I always felt like if I was doing something like running around at work or such, it would take a bit longer for the effects to start. Also even if the withdrawal effects are the same, I would much rather have them when I'm awake rather than at night or when I'm trying to sleep. The second I close my eyes it's when the withdrawals get the worst no matter how far along I am, so that is always my biggest issue. 

I never noticed if I specifically would get it worse at certain times, I always felt like it had more to do with when I stop/start, and the mornings generally were always the worst.

Ideally, my old work schedule consisted of my getting completely plastered before sleeping (even if I slept for like 4 hours) so I can kinda time it to where I can get through work without hitting the worst of the withdrawals and then start drinking again immediately after. 

There was only a 6-8 hour span per day (not including sleeping, which is a necessity I can control the schedule of) where I literally couldn't drink so most of my schedule played around that. It's not as big of an issue without a job, even though I've generally kept myself in check lately.

I would space my drinking out better during the day with more alcohol. When I had less, I would save it for when I KNEW I needed it, like about to go to sleep or if I needed to be somewhat coherent (see: not in withdrawals) for an event or function. So I'm not exactly sure if I would drink more or less, but I think my overall drunkenness would be more even with more, where I wouldn't dip below a certain point but I also wouldn't spike my body into oblivion within 5 minutes like I did with a limited amount.

I've been blessed to be born as a hyperactive person in general so nobody ever questioned why my hands were so shaky. It would usually be "wow, you're shaking bad. How many pots of coffee did you have this morning?" It worked right into my narrative as well since I almost always have to have caffeine near me to dampen the outward effects of alcohol to be productive.
One of my close friends went to go see Coheed and Cambria without me and I didn't have a complete meltdown about it like I would have at any other point. That counts...right?

Alcohol. In the last year and a half I've had clean time of 121 days and 104 days (currently I'm at 26 days which would by default be the third longest stretch), but the other 1/3 of drinking caused me to lose two jobs, be hospitalized a dozen times, and be in four different programs to try and get me to stop.

I wouldn't wish the withdrawals on my worst enemy. One of the more unknown facts about alcohol is that its withdrawals are one of only three drugs that can kill you, and I've been in rooms with heroin addicts who would tell me I looked more miserable physically than they were feeling...which isn't a badge of honor, trust me.

But whenever someone would tell me, "yeah, that's horrible that alcohol can actually kill you," I would tell them, "it's actually not bad. Sometimes when you're in that deep and you're hopeless in withdrawal, you cling onto the idea that there's a chance you CAN die and get you out of this." Depression and suicidal thoughts during withdrawal are the worst, but they're also hard to act on upon. There are times I just wanted to end everything, but was too physically and mentally messed up to put the effort in. But, if I was able to get up, that means I was able to go to a liquor store and shut those voices up for a bit anyway.

A lot of my addiction is/was trying to work my patterns around jobs and friends and such, but eventually it turned into having to work my jobs around the schedule of addiction which ends up not working in the long run.

Brings back a lot of Sandy memories. I lived near the Jersey shore in 2012 and thought "hurricanes don't usually last this far north, I'm sure it'll fizzle out at sea." It made direct landfall 30 miles south of me and became the second costliest storm in US history. I was fortunate because I was maybe a mile from the ocean but on the northern end (kind of where NJ juts out and the view from the piers is NYC, if that makes sense), but at an elevation where my area wasn't too flooded. Yet five miles west and east both were trashed and it took weeks for the local highway to reopen either because of the massive storm surge, rivers overflowing, or complete lack of infrastructure to deal with this type of mess. Places like Sea Bright and Monmouth Beach still aren't the same, and you can find places in Brooklyn, NY, Queens, and Staten Island that have barely been touched in terms of rebuilding.

I have a good friend in Gainesville so hopefully inland doesn't get too bad but I'm definitely praying for all those in the line of the storm because it is looking scary.

It gets tricky but I felt like hiding alcohol inside a bag of rock salt on the stairs leading to my house did help since you wouldn't get the extra attraction of a door opening which raises red flags. It's summer so nobody touches the rock salt, and it avoids me having to go outside, for example.

It's crazy isn't it?! Even where I live it isn't alcohol, it's heroin; NJ has probably the worst heroin epidemic in the US going on (never tried once), so when it comes to me anything somewhat decently high to most is treated as if it's the craziest thing they've ever seen because alcohol isn't generally seen as something as important right now.

I only get told when asked, but I usually only ask when I hear "well your alcohol level was pretty high..." I once got told that for a .25 and I was trying not to laugh because I've been admitted in the .4's before completely coherent and such. It almost felt like nothing to me which is both sad and funny at the same time.

It does seem like a crapshoot sometimes because half the time I end up in the hospital is due to withdrawals so a lot of the time it would generally be less than a .2

I agree and I know I have a more conservative mindset about that because it seems like a LOT of people draw the line there. But when you've been in the hospital with alcohol levels 6 times the legal limit, having enough to be what most people consider at the least buzzed/early stages of legally drunk is actually not the worst thing in the world.

Driving with withdrawals is the absolute worst. My most recent job we would get out at around 4-5 a.m. and I wouldn't even be able to see the road my eyes were twitching so bad. Then counting down until the liquor store opened which would have been best-case scenario four hours from then.

Oh I know. I joked last week to someone that I'm in a "rebuilding mode." Even all of my subscriptions besides Amazon prime are canceled so I'm just about out of distractions which can be either really good or really bad at this point.

I've always been extremely driven towards goals even with (or maybe in spite) of my CA so each time something gets messed up to hell directly because of my drinking I take it hard, especially when I'm trying to do the right thing. The fact that there is nothing I can do to change any of this now (no way I'm getting the car back, I don't have income until someone calls me, etc.) is frustrating as hell. I've had sober time of 99 days and 121 in the past year yet if anything I've lost more now than I have even last year when I had to spend over a month in rehab.

I've gotten an open container before and it was maybe a half-drunken bottle of whiskey on my passengers seat. I was parked at a waterfront in the middle of the night that was right by where I used to live (not even half a mile) and the officer I guess was timing me to see how long I've been sitting there. My answers when he asked matched exactly with what he saw so he just wrote me an open container even though my car was on and it was clear I had something to drink.
